summary: NexAris is a web application developed to detect and track moving celestial objects using images from NASA's SPHEREx mission. Our system analyzes its 102 infrared spectral channels to identify objects that change position across observations. We retrieve data from NASA's IPAC Infrared Science Archive and integrate complementary sky imagery through Aladin Lite, including visible light and near-infrared surveys, alongside mid-infrared images from the AIIWISE survey. We reduce observational noise, detect potential moving objects, and cross-match them with astronomical catalogs and databases, including Gaia, NASA/JPL Small Body Database, and the IAU Minor Planet Center, to identify known objects. Unmatched candidates are flagged for further investigation and potential discovery. What distinguishes NexAris is its ability to generate results dynamically, combined with a AI chatbot and an interactive, age-adaptive educational game that introduces infrared astronomy to people of different ages and levels of scientific knowledge.
details:
NexAris is a full-stack astronomical application that combines multi-band infrared image processing, moving-object detection, astronomical catalog cross-matching, and interactive education. The system uses actual observations from NASA's SPHEREx mission, analyzing all 102 infrared spectral bands to identify celestial objects that change position across observations. Through direct API integration with NASA's IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), NexAris retrieves and downloads FITS image for analysis.

At the core of the application is GhostShift, our Python-based data processing pipeline. It uses image registration, image subtraction, source detection, and positional comparison to identify potential moving objects across different observation times. The pipeline combines information from multiple infrared bands, with particular attention to the 1.1-1.56 μm wavelength range, to help distinguish potential moving objects from background stars and galaxies. It also accounts for background noise, cosmic rays, and image artifacts to reduce false detections. Detected objects are then cross matched automatically against astronomical catalogs, including ESA Gaia, NASA/JPL Small Body Database, and the IAU Minor Planet Center, using celestial coordinates, observation timestamps, and predicted orbital positions. Objects without a matching catalog entry are flagged and color coded as unknown moving objects for further investigation and potential discovery.

NexAris also provides an interactive Sky Explorer powered by Aladin Lite, integrating DSS2 Visible light, 2MASS near-infrared, and AIIWISE mid-infrared sky surveys. Users can enter celestial coordinates, smoothly switch between different wavelength observations, and explore detected objects directly on the sky map. Selecting an object reveals its identification, detection time, motion description, positional coordinates, signal accuracy, and links to the MPC and JPL databases for further investigation.

Beyond scientific exploration, NexAris includes an interactive educational game called NexAris Odyssey designed for different age groups and levels of scientific knowledge. Players guide a rocket through obstacles by answering questions about infrared astronomy, the relationship between temperature and infrared radiation, the characteristics of different spectral bands, and planets. The experience adapts to its audience, introducing foundational concepts to children and high school students while offering more advanced exploration and actual object detection opportunities for university students and experts.

We developed the platform using GoDaddy, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Next.js, with Python powering the GhostShift processing pipeline. Figma was used for UI/UX design and prototyping, Cloudflare R2 for data storage, Vercel for hosting and automated deployment, and GitHub for version control and team collaboration. Aladin Lite provides astronomical visualization and access to complementary sky surveys.

The main challenges we considered were handling large astronomical datasets, processing multiple spectral bands, reducing false positives, maintaining reliable object identification, and balancing processing performance with scientific accuracy. We also prioritized accessibility and usability ensuring that complex astronomical observations could be explored by both specialists and people with no prior astronomy background.

What makes NexAris creative is its combination of scientific data processing, multi-wavelength exploration, automated object identification, and age-adaptive education through our NexAris Odyssey game within a single platform. Our intended impact is to make infrared astronomy and moving object investigation more accessible, support the identification of potentially unknown celestial objects, and encourage scientific discovery beyond professional research environments. Looking ahead, we aim to integrate NexAris directly with astronomical observation platforms such as Aladin Lite, expand its catalog integration, further develop its astronomy chatbot, and introduce the platform to local and international observatory centers as an educational and scientific exploration tool. We also intent to add a 3D view and let the users report interesting movers to make the tool more interactive.
